name: Ad Hominem
hook: Why are we listening to Dr. Patel on climate policy? She got divorced twice — clearly can't make sound judgements.
oneLiner: Attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself.
deepDive: Ad hominem swaps the target of a debate from the claim to the claimant. Instead of showing that an argument is wrong, it tries to make the audience distrust the person, so the argument gets dismissed by association. It works because we intuitively treat 'who said it' as a shortcut for 'is it true' — but a claim's truth doesn't depend on the character, history, or motives of whoever raised it. The tell is a sudden pivot from the topic to the person: the moment biography, lifestyle, or past mistakes appear in place of evidence, the argument has been abandoned. Note the legitimate exception — challenging someone's credibility is fair when their reliability is *directly* the issue (a conflict of interest, a relevant track record). Ad hominem is when the personal fact is irrelevant to the claim.
howToSpot: The reply targets the person's character, background, or lifestyle instead of their point
Irrelevant personal history is dragged in — divorces, old failures, appearance, group membership
The actual claim is never engaged with; 'winning' means discrediting the speaker

examples.text: "We should listen to scientists on global warming." — "Why should we listen to you? You failed science in school."
examples.explanation: The speaker's past grades have no bearing on whether the scientific consensus is correct.

examples.text: "Here's my proposal for healthcare reform." — "We shouldn't listen to you, you're not even a doctor."
examples.explanation: Not being a doctor doesn't automatically make a policy proposal wrong — the proposal's merits are untouched.

examples.text: "This property tax could ease housing inequality." — "Of course she'd say that, she's a career economist who's never built anything."
examples.explanation: Her biography is used to dismiss the policy without addressing whether the tax is actually well-designed.

refutation.title: Name the move
refutation.text: Point out that the attack is aimed at the person, not the point.
refutation.comeback: That's about me, not the argument. What specifically is wrong with the evidence?

refutation.title: Redirect to the claim
refutation.text: Steer straight back to the original point and ask for a substantive response.
refutation.comeback: Set my background aside — can you give me a reason the policy itself doesn't work?

refutation.title: Separate credibility from truth
refutation.text: If they raise a relevant credibility concern, grant it but note it doesn't settle the claim.
refutation.comeback: Even if you're right about me, that doesn't make the data false. Let's look at the data.

avoidance: Attack arguments, never people — critique the reasoning, not the reasoner
Before dismissing a source, ask whether the personal fact is actually relevant to the claim
Notice when you're tempted to bring up someone's history instead of their point

name: Straw Man
hook: So you want stricter gun laws? So you basically want to leave every family defenceless.
oneLiner: Misrepresenting someone's argument to make it easier to attack.
deepDive: A straw man replaces the opponent's real position with a distorted, exaggerated, or oversimplified version — the 'straw' figure — then knocks that down instead. It feels like a rebuttal, but nothing the person actually said has been addressed. It's persuasive because the caricature is usually easier to dislike than the real claim: 'sensible firearm regulation' becomes 'confiscating everyone's guns.' The pattern to watch for is a restatement that's more extreme, more absolute, or more sinister than the original — words like 'so you're saying', 'basically', or 'you just want' often introduce the swap. Note it can be deployed deliberately as a bad-faith tactic to bait an opponent, or committed accidentally by someone who genuinely misheard. Either way the fix is the same: refuse to defend a position you never held.
howToSpot: Your position gets restated in a more extreme or absolute form than you meant
Phrases like 'so you're saying...', 'basically you want...', 'you just hate...' precede the distortion
They attack a version of your view you don't actually hold — and never quote what you said

examples.text: "We need stricter firearm regulations." — "So you want to take everyone's guns and leave us defenceless?"
examples.explanation: Regulation isn't confiscation; the reply attacks a position the speaker never took.

examples.text: "We should invest more in public transport." — "You just hate cars and want to force everyone onto buses."
examples.explanation: Investing in one option isn't banning another — the real, moderate claim is swapped for an extreme one.

examples.text: "I think the essay needs a stronger conclusion." — "Oh, so the whole thing is garbage to you?"
examples.explanation: A targeted critique of one section is inflated into a sweeping condemnation of the whole.

refutation.title: Restate your actual position
refutation.text: Calmly correct the distortion and put your real claim back on the table.
refutation.comeback: That's not what I said. My actual point was narrower — let me restate it clearly.

refutation.title: Name the misrepresentation
refutation.text: Point out that they're arguing against a version you don't hold.
refutation.comeback: You're attacking a position I never took. Can you respond to what I actually argued?

refutation.title: Ask them to engage the real claim
refutation.text: Put the burden back on them to address your genuine point.
refutation.comeback: Set the exaggerated version aside — what's your objection to the specific thing I proposed?

avoidance: Restate an opponent's view in a form they'd agree with before you critique it
Steelman: engage the strongest version of the argument, not the weakest
If you catch yourself adding 'basically' or 'so you're saying', check you're not distorting

name: Tu Quoque (You Too)
hook: You're telling me to stop smoking? You smoked for ten years!
oneLiner: Deflecting criticism by pointing to the critic's own hypocrisy instead of answering it.
deepDive: Tu quoque ('you too') dodges a claim by accusing the person making it of not living up to it. The hidden assumption is that a hypocrite's argument must be false — but a claim's truth is completely independent of whether the speaker practises what they preach. A chain smoker telling you smoking is dangerous is still right about the danger. It's a close cousin of whataboutism, but tu quoque specifically targets the *speaker's* consistency, whereas whataboutism deflects to an unrelated topic. Spot it by the structure: the response starts with 'but you...' or 'what about when you...' and never actually engages the point. The inconsistency might be a fair thing to raise separately — but it doesn't refute the argument.
howToSpot: The reply opens with 'but you...' or 'what about when you did...'
It points at the critic's behaviour instead of the substance of the criticism
The original claim is left completely unaddressed

examples.text: "You shouldn't eat so much junk food." — "You had McDonald's twice last week, so don't lecture me."
examples.explanation: Whether the adviser is consistent has no bearing on whether the advice is correct.

examples.text: "We need to cut carbon emissions." — "You drive a car every day — you're a hypocrite."
examples.explanation: The speaker's car use doesn't change the science on emissions; the claim stands or falls on its own.

examples.text: "You really should apologise to her." — "You never apologise for anything!"
examples.explanation: Even if true, the critic's own failings don't determine whether an apology is warranted here.

refutation.title: Separate the messenger from the message
refutation.text: Grant the inconsistency but point out it doesn't touch the claim.
refutation.comeback: Even if I'm inconsistent, does that make what I said wrong?

refutation.title: Redirect to the point
refutation.text: Bring the conversation back to the actual argument.
refutation.comeback: My behaviour is a separate issue. Let's focus on whether the point itself holds.

refutation.title: Concede and continue
refutation.text: Acknowledge the hypocrisy openly, then refuse to let it end the discussion.
refutation.comeback: You're right that I should change too — but that doesn't address whether the argument is sound.

avoidance: Judge an argument on its merits, not on the arguer's consistency
If you spot hypocrisy, raise it as a separate point rather than a rebuttal
Don't let 'but you do it too' stop you from engaging the actual claim

name: Red Herring
hook: You're worried about the missed deadline? Do you know how stressful my week has been?
oneLiner: Introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the real issue.
deepDive: A red herring drags a fresh, unrelated (but often emotionally engaging) subject across the trail so the original question gets lost. Unlike a straw man, it doesn't distort your argument — it simply changes the subject to something that feels connected but isn't. It works because the new topic is usually more vivid or more sympathetic, and audiences follow the movement. The tell is a shift that sounds like a response but doesn't actually bear on the point: the conversation ends up somewhere entirely different, and the original question is never answered. The fix is to notice the swap and refuse to chase it: acknowledge the new topic if you must, but anchor firmly back to what was actually asked.
howToSpot: The reply changes the subject to something that only feels related
The new topic is often more emotional or dramatic than the original question
By the end, the original point has quietly gone unanswered

examples.text: "Why was the budget report late again?" — "Do you have any idea how much pressure the whole team is under right now?"
examples.explanation: Team stress may be real, but it doesn't answer the specific question about the late report.

examples.text: "The new policy raises costs for tenants." — "But think about how much landlords have suffered this decade."
examples.explanation: Landlord hardship is a different topic; it sidesteps the actual claim about tenant costs.

examples.text: "You promised to fix the bug by Friday." — "Well, the whole codebase is a mess anyway, whose fault is that?"
examples.explanation: The state of the codebase distracts from the unmet, specific commitment.

refutation.title: Flag the detour
refutation.text: Note that the topic has shifted and the original point is still open.
refutation.comeback: That's a separate issue. I still want to come back to the original question.

refutation.title: Park it, don't chase it
refutation.text: Offer to discuss the new topic later, but hold the line now.
refutation.comeback: Happy to talk about that afterwards — but first, can we resolve the point I raised?

refutation.title: Repeat the question
refutation.text: Simply restate the original question, unmoved by the diversion.
refutation.comeback: I hear you, but the question was specifically about the deadline. What happened there?

avoidance: When answering, make sure your response actually addresses the question asked
Notice the urge to pivot to a topic where you're more comfortable
Finish one thread before opening another

name: False Dichotomy
hook: Either we cut the entire arts budget, or the whole city goes bankrupt. Pick one.
oneLiner: Presenting only two options when more actually exist.
deepDive: A false dichotomy compresses a spectrum of possibilities into just two — usually one the speaker wants and one nobody wants — so the desired choice looks inevitable. It's powerful because it feels decisive and simplifies a hard decision, but it hides the middle ground, the combinations, and the third options entirely. The reasoning smuggles in a hidden premise ('these are the only two choices') that's almost never true. Watch for framing words like 'either/or', 'if you're not with us you're against us', and any argument that treats a compromise or a third path as if it doesn't exist. The counter is almost always to name the missing options — the moment a third choice is on the table, the forced choice collapses.
howToSpot: Only two options are offered, framed as exhaustive ('either X or Y')
One option is obviously bad, making the other look inevitable
Middle-ground positions, combinations, or third options are ignored

examples.text: "Either we cut all environmental regulations or the economy collapses."
examples.explanation: There's a wide range of regulatory levels between 'all' and 'none' — the two extremes aren't the only choices.

examples.text: "You're either with us or against us."
examples.explanation: This erases neutrality, partial agreement, and conditional support, forcing a binary that rarely reflects reality.

examples.text: "We either ban the phones entirely or accept that grades will keep falling."
examples.explanation: Limited use, time restrictions, and other policies exist between a total ban and doing nothing.

refutation.title: Name the third option
refutation.text: Point out at least one possibility the framing left out.
refutation.comeback: Those aren't the only two choices — there's a middle path here, for example…

refutation.title: Reject the forced choice
refutation.text: Refuse the binary and ask why the options were limited to two.
refutation.comeback: Why do these have to be the only options? I don't accept that framing.

refutation.title: Show the spectrum
refutation.text: Reframe the issue as a range rather than a switch.
refutation.comeback: This isn't all-or-nothing — it's a question of how much, and where we draw the line.

avoidance: Ask 'are these really the only options?' before accepting a two-way choice
Look for middle-ground and combination solutions
Be wary of 'either/or' framing, especially when one option is clearly unappealing

name: Slippery Slope
hook: If we let students redo one exam, next they'll expect to redo everything, and soon grades will mean nothing.
oneLiner: Claiming one small step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome, without justifying the chain.
deepDive: A slippery slope argues that permitting a modest first step will unavoidably cascade into a disastrous end state — but it never justifies the links in that chain. Each 'and then' is asserted, not demonstrated. It's persuasive because the final outcome is scary and the chain sounds superficially plausible, so the fear does the work that evidence should. The key distinction: a slope argument is only a fallacy when the causal chain is unsupported. If you can show that each step genuinely and predictably leads to the next, it becomes a legitimate risk argument. So the test is always the same — ask for the mechanism connecting each step, and watch how quickly the chain falls apart when it has to be defended rather than merely asserted.
howToSpot: A modest proposal is said to lead 'inevitably' to an extreme result
The chain of steps is asserted but never actually justified
The scary end-point does the persuading, not evidence for each link

examples.text: "If we allow same-day returns, soon people will abuse it, then we'll lose all profit, then we'll go under."
examples.explanation: Each step is possible but none is shown to follow necessarily from the last — the chain is assumed, not argued.

examples.text: "Legalise this one drug and before long everything will be legal and society will collapse."
examples.explanation: There's no mechanism given for why one specific policy forces every other domino to fall.

examples.text: "If I let you leave early today, I'll have to let everyone leave early every day."
examples.explanation: A single exception doesn't automatically become an unbreakable universal rule.

refutation.title: Ask for the mechanism
refutation.text: Request evidence for each link in the chain, not just the ending.
refutation.comeback: What actually makes step one lead to step two? Walk me through the connection.

refutation.title: Break the chain
refutation.text: Point out where a step could easily not follow.
refutation.comeback: That first step doesn't force the next — we can allow this and still stop there.

refutation.title: Distinguish risk from inevitability
refutation.text: Grant a real risk but reject the claim of certainty.
refutation.comeback: There's a risk worth managing, sure — but 'possible' isn't 'inevitable.'

avoidance: When predicting consequences, justify each step rather than asserting a chain
Distinguish 'this could lead to' from 'this will inevitably lead to'
Evaluate a proposal on its own merits before imagining worst-case cascades

name: Appeal to Authority
hook: A celebrity doctor endorsed this supplement, so it must work.
oneLiner: Claiming something is true just because an authority figure said so.
deepDive: This fallacy treats a claim as proven because an authority asserted it — but expertise is evidence, not proof, and it only counts when the authority is speaking within their genuine field of expertise and reflects a real consensus. It goes wrong in three common ways: the authority is outside their domain (a physicist on nutrition), the authority is misrepresented or cherry-picked against a broader consensus, or 'authority' is just fame or confidence with no real expertise behind it. Legitimate deference to experts isn't fallacious; the fallacy is substituting the label of authority for the reasoning and evidence that authority is supposed to be summarising. Ask what the expert actually knows, whether it's their field, and whether other experts agree.
howToSpot: 'An expert said so' is offered in place of the actual evidence or reasoning
The authority is speaking outside their real area of expertise
A single authority is cited against, or without checking, the wider consensus

examples.text: "A famous physicist says this diet cures disease, so it must be true."
examples.explanation: Physics expertise doesn't transfer to medicine — this is authority borrowed from the wrong field.

examples.text: "My professor believes it, and she's brilliant, so the theory has to be right."
examples.explanation: Brilliance in general, or even in a field, doesn't make an individual claim correct without supporting evidence.

examples.text: "This influencer has millions of followers and swears by it, so it works."
examples.explanation: Popularity and reach are not expertise; a large audience is not evidence.

refutation.title: Ask for the evidence
refutation.text: Request the reasoning behind the claim, not just the credential.
refutation.comeback: What's the actual evidence they're basing that on?

refutation.title: Check the domain
refutation.text: Point out when the authority is outside their expertise.
refutation.comeback: That's not really their field — what do specialists in this area say?

refutation.title: Appeal to consensus, not one voice
refutation.text: Ask whether the wider body of experts agrees.
refutation.comeback: Is that the general view among experts, or just one person's take?

avoidance: Use authority as a starting point, then look for the underlying evidence
Check that the expert is speaking within their field
Prefer expert consensus over any single confident voice

name: Hasty Generalization
hook: I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there must be rude.
oneLiner: Drawing a broad conclusion from too small or unrepresentative a sample.
deepDive: A hasty generalization leaps from a handful of cases — sometimes a single one — to a sweeping rule about a whole group or category. It's a natural shortcut: our brains generalise from limited experience constantly. It becomes a fallacy when the sample is too small, cherry-picked, or unrepresentative to support the size of the claim. The danger is that the conclusion feels earned ('I've seen it with my own eyes') while resting on almost no data. Watch for words like 'all', 'always', 'never', or 'those people' attached to evidence that amounts to a couple of anecdotes. The fix is to ask how many cases the conclusion rests on and whether they're representative of the whole.
howToSpot: A sweeping claim ('all', 'always', 'those people') rests on very few cases
The examples are anecdotal, cherry-picked, or unrepresentative
Personal experience is treated as proof of a universal rule

examples.text: "My two friends who tried remote work were unproductive, so remote work doesn't work."
examples.explanation: Two cases can't support a conclusion about remote work in general.

examples.text: "This one study found no effect, so the whole theory is debunked."
examples.explanation: A single study is rarely enough to overturn a body of evidence.

examples.text: "The last three startups I saw fail were all in fintech — clearly fintech is doomed."
examples.explanation: A tiny, selective sample is being stretched into a claim about an entire sector.

refutation.title: Question the sample size
refutation.text: Ask how many cases the conclusion actually rests on.
refutation.comeback: How many examples is that based on? A couple of cases can't tell us about everyone.

refutation.title: Ask about representativeness
refutation.text: Probe whether the examples reflect the whole group.
refutation.comeback: Were those cases typical, or just the ones that stood out?

refutation.title: Request stronger data
refutation.text: Ask for evidence proportional to the size of the claim.
refutation.comeback: Is there broader data on this, rather than a few anecdotes?

avoidance: Match the strength of your conclusion to the amount of evidence
Be suspicious of 'all' and 'always' when the evidence is a handful of stories
Ask whether your examples are representative before generalising

name: Appeal to Emotion
hook: If you really cared about children, you wouldn't even ask about the cost.
oneLiner: Using feelings — fear, pity, anger — in place of evidence to win an argument.
deepDive: An appeal to emotion tries to move you to a conclusion by stirring a feeling rather than giving a reason. Emotions aren't irrelevant to arguments — it's fine to care about outcomes — but the fallacy is when emotion *replaces* the logical case instead of accompanying it. Fear, pity, guilt, and outrage are used because they bypass scrutiny: a frightened or guilty audience is less likely to ask for evidence. The tell is that when you strip the emotional language away, there's no argument left underneath — just a feeling pointed at a conclusion. The fix is to acknowledge the emotion as real, then ask what the actual evidence for the claim is, separate from how it makes you feel.
howToSpot: Vivid emotional language stands in for evidence or reasoning
You're made to feel guilty, afraid, or heartless for even questioning the claim
Strip out the feelings and no actual argument remains

examples.text: "Think of the children! How can you oppose this bill and still sleep at night?"
examples.explanation: Guilt is used to shut down scrutiny rather than to show the bill actually works.

examples.text: "After everything I've done for this company, you'd really deny me this?"
examples.explanation: An appeal to pity replaces the question of whether the request is justified on its merits.

examples.text: "If you don't share this, you clearly don't care about the cause."
examples.explanation: Fear of looking uncaring is used to pressure action, with no argument for the action itself.

refutation.title: Acknowledge the feeling
refutation.text: Validate the emotion, then separate it from the claim.
refutation.comeback: I do care about this — and precisely because I do, I want to check it actually works.

refutation.title: Ask for the evidence
refutation.text: Request the reasoning underneath the emotional appeal.
refutation.comeback: Setting the feelings aside for a second, what's the actual case for this?

refutation.title: Name the pressure
refutation.text: Point out that emotion is being used to avoid scrutiny.
refutation.comeback: Making me feel guilty doesn't answer whether the proposal is sound.

avoidance: Notice when a strong feeling is standing in for a reason
Let emotion inform your values, but demand evidence for factual claims
Be wary of arguments that make questioning them feel morally wrong

name: Circular Reasoning
hook: This book is trustworthy because it says right there that everything in it is true.
oneLiner: Using the conclusion as its own evidence, so the argument goes in a circle.
deepDive: Circular reasoning assumes the very thing it's trying to prove — the conclusion is smuggled in as a premise, so the argument never actually establishes anything. It can be hard to spot because it often sounds like an explanation: 'X is true because X is true' gets dressed up in different words at each end of the circle. The reason it's a fallacy is that it provides no independent support; if you already doubted the conclusion, the argument gives you no new reason to accept it. The test is to ask whether the premise would convince someone who doesn't already believe the conclusion. If the only support for a claim is a restatement of the claim, the circle is closed and empty.
howToSpot: The premise and the conclusion are really the same statement in different words
The reason offered only makes sense if you already accept the conclusion
No independent evidence is ever introduced

examples.text: "He's the most honest person I know because he'd never lie to me."
examples.explanation: Never lying is just a restatement of being honest — no independent reason is given.

examples.text: "The policy is the right one because it's what a reasonable person would choose."
examples.explanation: Calling the choice 'reasonable' assumes the conclusion it's meant to support.

examples.text: "We know the ad works because sales went up, and sales went up because the ad works."
examples.explanation: Each half leans on the other; nothing outside the loop supports either claim.

refutation.title: Expose the loop
refutation.text: Show that the premise and conclusion are the same claim.
refutation.comeback: That's just restating your conclusion — what independent reason supports it?

refutation.title: Ask for outside evidence
refutation.text: Request support that doesn't assume the point.
refutation.comeback: Is there any evidence for this that doesn't already assume it's true?

refutation.title: Test on a skeptic
refutation.text: Point out the argument only works on people who already agree.
refutation.comeback: Would this convince someone who doesn't already believe it? I don't think it would.

avoidance: Check that your premises don't secretly assume your conclusion
Support claims with independent evidence, not restatements
Ask whether your reasoning would persuade someone who disagrees

name: Appeal to Tradition
hook: We've always done onboarding this way, so there's no reason to change it.
oneLiner: Claiming something is right or best simply because it's how things have always been done.
deepDive: This fallacy treats age or longevity as proof of merit — 'we've always done it this way' becomes a reason not to question or change something. But how long a practice has existed says nothing about whether it's effective, ethical, or optimal; plenty of long-standing traditions were also long-standing mistakes. Tradition can carry real accumulated wisdom, so it's not worthless as a consideration — but it's a starting hypothesis, not a conclusion. The fallacy is when 'it's traditional' ends the discussion instead of opening it. The counter is to ask why the practice works, not how old it is: if there's a good reason, the reason will stand on its own without needing the appeal to history.
howToSpot: Age or 'the way it's always been' is offered as the reason something is right
Change is resisted purely because the current way is established
No case is made for why the traditional way is actually better

examples.text: "Marriage has always meant this, so it can never mean anything else."
examples.explanation: Longevity of a definition doesn't establish that it's the only valid one.

examples.text: "Our company has never offered remote work, so we shouldn't start now."
examples.explanation: Never having done something isn't a reason it wouldn't work — only that it's untried here.

examples.text: "This ritual has been performed for centuries; questioning it is disrespectful."
examples.explanation: Age is used to shield the practice from the question of whether it still serves a purpose.

refutation.title: Ask why, not how long
refutation.text: Redirect from the age of the practice to its justification.
refutation.comeback: How long we've done it isn't the point — what makes it the right approach today?

refutation.title: Separate wisdom from habit
refutation.text: Grant tradition may hold value, then ask what that value is.
refutation.comeback: There may be good reasons behind this — can we name them, rather than just its age?

refutation.title: Test against the goal
refutation.text: Ask whether the tradition still serves its purpose.
refutation.comeback: Does it still achieve what we actually want, or are we just repeating it?

avoidance: Ask why a practice works, not just how long it's existed
Treat 'we've always done it this way' as a question, not an answer
Judge traditions by their current merits and outcomes

name: Bandwagon Fallacy
hook: Everyone's investing in this coin — you're crazy not to be in.
oneLiner: Claiming something is true or good because lots of people believe it or do it.
deepDive: The bandwagon fallacy treats popularity as evidence: if enough people believe or do something, it must be right. But the number of people holding a view is independent of whether the view is correct — majorities have been wrong throughout history, and popularity is often driven by hype, social pressure, or marketing rather than truth. It exploits our real and useful instinct to follow the crowd (which is a decent heuristic in genuinely uncertain, low-stakes situations) and misapplies it to questions that should be settled by evidence. The tell is 'everyone', 'nobody', or a headcount used in place of a reason. The counter is to ask what the crowd actually knows, and whether their belief is based on evidence or just on each other.
howToSpot: 'Everyone believes/does it' is offered as the reason it's correct
Social proof or headcounts replace evidence
Pressure to conform substitutes for a genuine argument

examples.text: "Millions of people can't be wrong about this product."
examples.explanation: Popularity can be manufactured by marketing; large numbers don't guarantee quality.

examples.text: "Everyone in the office thinks the plan is fine, so it must be."
examples.explanation: Shared opinion isn't evidence — the whole group could be missing the same flaw.

examples.text: "All my friends are dropping the class, so it's obviously a bad course."
examples.explanation: A cluster of like-minded people copying each other isn't an independent judgement.

refutation.title: Separate popular from true
refutation.text: Point out that agreement isn't evidence.
refutation.comeback: Lots of people believing it doesn't make it true — what's the actual reason?

refutation.title: Ask what the crowd knows
refutation.text: Probe whether the majority's belief rests on evidence.
refutation.comeback: Are they basing that on evidence, or just on each other?

refutation.title: Cite counter-examples
refutation.text: Recall that majorities have often been wrong.
refutation.comeback: Plenty of popular beliefs have turned out false — popularity isn't a guarantee.

avoidance: Ask whether a popular belief rests on evidence or just on numbers
Be willing to hold a minority view when the evidence supports it
Notice when you're agreeing to fit in rather than because you're convinced

name: False Cause
hook: I wore my lucky socks and we won — so the socks won us the game.
oneLiner: Assuming that because one thing followed another, the first caused the second.
deepDive: False cause treats sequence or correlation as proof of causation: B happened after A, so A must have caused B. But two things can co-occur for many reasons — coincidence, a shared third cause, or reverse causation — none of which involve A causing B. It's a deeply intuitive error because our minds are built to detect causes, and a story where A causes B is more satisfying than 'it's complicated.' The classic form is 'post hoc': it happened after, therefore because of. The fix is to ask whether there's an actual mechanism linking the two, whether something else could explain both, and whether the correlation holds up beyond the one instance. Correlation is a reason to investigate a cause, never proof of one.
howToSpot: A causal claim rests only on one thing happening after another
No mechanism is given for how A would actually cause B
Alternative explanations (coincidence, a third factor) are never considered

examples.text: "Crime rose the same year we opened the new park, so the park caused it."
examples.explanation: Two things rising together doesn't mean one caused the other — many factors move at once.

examples.text: "I started taking this vitamin and my cold went away, so it cured me."
examples.explanation: Colds resolve on their own; the timing doesn't establish the vitamin did anything.

examples.text: "Every time I wash my car it rains, so washing my car causes rain."
examples.explanation: A memorable coincidence is mistaken for a causal link with no plausible mechanism.

refutation.title: Ask for the mechanism
refutation.text: Request how, exactly, A would cause B.
refutation.comeback: What's the actual mechanism connecting these two? Timing alone isn't enough.

refutation.title: Raise alternatives
refutation.text: Suggest coincidence or a hidden third cause.
refutation.comeback: Could something else be causing both — or is this just coincidence?

refutation.title: Distinguish correlation from cause
refutation.text: State the principle directly.
refutation.comeback: They happened together, but that doesn't tell us one caused the other.

avoidance: Ask whether a correlation might be coincidence or a shared cause
Look for a plausible mechanism before claiming causation
Remember 'after' does not mean 'because of'

name: Genetic Fallacy
hook: That idea came from a tabloid, so it can't possibly be true.
oneLiner: Judging a claim as true or false based on its origin rather than its content.
deepDive: The genetic fallacy evaluates an idea by where it came from — its source, history, or the character of whoever first said it — instead of by whether it's actually correct. A good idea from a disreputable source is still good; a bad idea from a prestigious one is still bad. It overlaps with ad hominem but is broader: it applies to institutions, publications, origins, and traditions, not just people. It works because origin is a fast heuristic for credibility, and often a useful one — but a heuristic isn't a verdict. The tell is dismissing or accepting a claim purely on its pedigree ('that's just something the other party made up' / 'it came from a respected journal, so it's right'). The fix is to assess the claim on its own evidence, treating the source as a prompt to investigate rather than a conclusion.
howToSpot: A claim is accepted or rejected because of who or where it came from
The origin (a source, party, publication) is discussed instead of the content
No engagement with whether the claim is actually true

examples.text: "This health tip is nonsense — it came from a random blog."
examples.explanation: A dubious source can still be right; the tip should be checked on its own evidence.

examples.text: "That theory was originally proposed by a discredited scientist, so it's worthless."
examples.explanation: Ideas aren't permanently tainted by their origin — they stand or fall on their merits.

examples.text: "If the opposing party suggested it, it must be a bad policy."
examples.explanation: The source's identity is used to pre-judge the policy without examining it.

refutation.title: Separate source from claim
refutation.text: Note that origin doesn't determine truth.
refutation.comeback: Where it came from doesn't decide whether it's true — let's look at the claim itself.

refutation.title: Ask about the content
refutation.text: Redirect to the actual substance.
refutation.comeback: Set the source aside — is the claim itself right or wrong, and why?

refutation.title: Use the source as a prompt
refutation.text: Treat origin as a reason to verify, not to dismiss.
refutation.comeback: Fair to be skeptical of the source, so let's check the claim rather than reject it outright.

avoidance: Evaluate claims on their evidence, not their pedigree
Let a questionable source raise your scrutiny, not close the case
Don't accept a claim just because it comes from a prestigious source

name: No True Scotsman
hook: No real fan would ever criticise the band. — But I'm a fan and I did. — Then you're not a real fan.
oneLiner: Redefining a group on the spot to exclude any counter-example.
deepDive: This fallacy defends a sweeping generalisation about a group by redefining the group to expel any exception. When a counter-example appears ('here's a Scotsman who does that'), the claimant retreats to 'well, no *true* Scotsman would' — quietly changing the definition so the claim can never be falsified. It's a way of making a statement immune to evidence: whatever contradicts it is defined out of existence. The tell is the appearance of purity words — 'real', 'true', 'genuine' — right after a counter-example is raised. The counter is to pin down the definition *before* discussing exceptions, and to point out that a claim which reshapes itself to survive any counter-example isn't really making a testable claim at all.
howToSpot: A counter-example is met with 'no real/true/genuine [X] would...'
The definition of the group shifts precisely to exclude the exception
The claim is arranged so no evidence could ever disprove it

examples.text: "No true professional would miss a deadline." — "Sarah's a professional and she did." — "Then she's not truly professional."
examples.explanation: The definition of 'professional' is rewritten mid-argument to exclude the counter-example.

examples.text: "Real supporters never boo the team." — "Those were season-ticket holders booing." — "Real supporters wouldn't have."
examples.explanation: 'Real supporter' is redefined so that anyone who boos automatically doesn't count.

examples.text: "Genuine environmentalists don't fly." — "Many do, for conferences." — "Then they're not genuine."
examples.explanation: The category is purified on the spot to protect the original blanket claim.

refutation.title: Pin the definition first
refutation.text: Ask them to define the group before allowing exceptions.
refutation.comeback: Let's agree what counts as a 'real' one first — then we can test the claim.

refutation.title: Point out the moving target
refutation.text: Name the redefinition as it happens.
refutation.comeback: You've just changed the definition to exclude my example. That's not a fair test.

refutation.title: Ask what would count as disproof
refutation.text: Expose that the claim can't be falsified.
refutation.comeback: Is there any example that would count against your claim? If not, it isn't really testable.

avoidance: Define your terms before defending a generalisation about a group
When a counter-example appears, revise the claim, don't redefine the group
Notice when 'real' or 'true' is doing the work of dodging evidence

name: Loaded Question
hook: So, have you stopped cutting corners on your projects yet?
oneLiner: A question with a built-in assumption, so any direct answer admits something unproven.
deepDive: A loaded question smuggles an unproven (usually damaging) assumption into the question itself, so that any straightforward answer concedes the assumption. 'Have you stopped cutting corners?' traps you: 'yes' admits you did it before, 'no' admits you still do. The trick is that the presupposition was never established — it's slipped in as if already agreed. It's a favourite in interrogations, hostile interviews, and online pile-ons because it forces the target onto the back foot. The distinction from an ordinary pointed question is the hidden premise you never accepted. The counter is never to answer on the question's terms: expose and reject the presupposition first, then answer the legitimate part, if there is one.
howToSpot: Any direct yes/no answer forces you to concede something unproven
The question presupposes a fact that was never established
It's framed to put you on the defensive from the first word

examples.text: "Why do you always undermine the team in meetings?"
examples.explanation: It assumes you always undermine the team — answering 'why' concedes that you do.

examples.text: "Have you stopped wasting company money on this project?"
examples.explanation: Both 'yes' and 'no' admit you were wasting money, which was never shown.

examples.text: "When are you going to admit the whole plan was a mistake?"
examples.explanation: It presupposes the plan was a mistake and that you know it — neither is granted.

refutation.title: Reject the premise
refutation.text: Refuse to answer until the hidden assumption is addressed.
refutation.comeback: That question assumes something I don't accept — let's deal with that first.

refutation.title: Split the question
refutation.text: Separate the loaded part from any legitimate part.
refutation.comeback: There are two claims baked in there. I'll answer the fair one, but not the assumption.

refutation.title: Flip it back
refutation.text: Ask them to first establish the presupposition.
refutation.comeback: Before I answer, can you show that the thing you're assuming is even true?

avoidance: Check whether a question contains an assumption you haven't accepted
Ask neutral questions that don't presuppose their own answers
Address hidden premises before engaging with the surface question

name: Middle Ground Fallacy
hook: One scientist says the bridge is safe, one says it'll collapse — the truth must be somewhere in between.
oneLiner: Assuming the truth is always the compromise between two positions.
deepDive: This fallacy treats the midpoint between two views as automatically correct, as if truth were always a matter of splitting the difference. But sometimes one side is simply right and the other simply wrong, and 'meeting in the middle' just moves you toward the error. Compromise is a virtue in negotiation and values disputes; it's not a method for settling questions of fact. The fallacy is especially dangerous when one 'side' is an extreme or fabricated position deliberately staked out to drag the perceived centre toward it. The tell is 'the truth is somewhere in between' asserted without any evidence that the middle is actually where the evidence points. The counter is to insist that the answer be located by evidence, not by geometry.
howToSpot: 'The truth is somewhere in the middle' is stated as if it's automatically so
A compromise is treated as correct simply for being moderate
Evidence is ignored in favour of splitting the difference

examples.text: "Some say the earth is round, some say flat — probably it's a bit of both."
examples.explanation: There's no meaningful middle here; one position is factually correct and the other isn't.

examples.text: "He wants a full refund, I want to pay nothing, so half is obviously fair."
examples.explanation: Fairness depends on who's actually owed what, not on the arithmetic midpoint.

examples.text: "One report says the drug is safe, one fringe blog says it's deadly — the truth's in between."
examples.explanation: Averaging a rigorous study with a baseless claim doesn't produce truth.

refutation.title: Ask where the evidence points
refutation.text: Insist the answer be found by evidence, not position.
refutation.comeback: The middle isn't automatically right — where does the actual evidence land?

refutation.title: Check if one side is just wrong
refutation.text: Point out that sometimes there's no valid midpoint.
refutation.comeback: If one side is simply mistaken, compromising with it just moves us toward the error.

refutation.title: Expose manufactured extremes
refutation.text: Note when an extreme was staked out to drag the centre.
refutation.comeback: That extreme position looks designed to pull the 'middle' in its direction.

avoidance: Locate the truth with evidence, not by splitting the difference
Remember that sometimes one side is simply correct
Watch for extreme positions designed to shift the perceived centre

name: Equivocation
hook: Nothing is better than lifelong happiness. A cheese sandwich is better than nothing. So a cheese sandwich is better than lifelong happiness.
oneLiner: Using the same word in two different senses to make an argument seem to work.
deepDive: Equivocation exploits a word that has more than one meaning, sliding between the senses so that a conclusion appears to follow when it doesn't. The argument looks valid because the same word appears throughout — but the word means one thing in the premise and something else in the conclusion. It's the verbal equivalent of a bait-and-switch. Common culprits are words like 'right' (correct vs. entitlement), 'free' (no cost vs. liberty), 'theory' (hunch vs. scientific framework), and 'natural.' The tell is a conclusion that feels slippery or too clever, where re-reading reveals a key word has quietly changed meaning. The fix is to define the ambiguous term and hold it to one meaning throughout — the argument usually collapses once the word is pinned down.
howToSpot: A key word is used with two different meanings in the same argument
The conclusion only 'works' because of the shift in meaning
Pinning down a single definition makes the argument fall apart

examples.text: "Evolution is only a theory, and a theory is just a guess, so it's unproven."
examples.explanation: 'Theory' means a casual guess in one clause and a rigorous scientific framework in the other.

examples.text: "Everyone has the right to free speech, so this platform is violating my rights by moderating me."
examples.explanation: 'Right' as a legal protection against government is swapped for 'right' as an entitlement to any platform.

examples.text: "The sign says 'fine for parking here', so it must be fine to park here."
examples.explanation: 'Fine' shifts from a penalty to an approval between the sign and the conclusion.

refutation.title: Define the term
refutation.text: Ask for a single, fixed meaning of the slippery word.
refutation.comeback: Which meaning of that word are we using? Let's fix one and stick to it.

refutation.title: Expose the shift
refutation.text: Show where the meaning changes mid-argument.
refutation.comeback: The word means one thing in your premise and another in your conclusion.

refutation.title: Re-run with one meaning
refutation.text: Rebuild the argument holding the term constant.
refutation.comeback: If we use the same definition throughout, the conclusion doesn't actually follow.

avoidance: Define ambiguous terms and use them consistently
Re-read arguments to check a key word hasn't shifted meaning
Be alert to words with both an everyday and a technical sense

name: Burden of Proof Fallacy
hook: I say there's a secret cabal running the economy. Prove there isn't.
oneLiner: Demanding others disprove your claim instead of supporting it yourself.
deepDive: The burden of proof rests on whoever makes a claim, not on everyone else to refute it. This fallacy reverses that: someone asserts something, then insists you disprove it, treating your inability to do so as evidence they're right. But 'you can't prove me wrong' is not the same as 'I'm right' — especially for unfalsifiable or extraordinary claims, where disproof is impossible by design. It's a favourite of conspiracy theories and pseudoscience because it offloads the hard work of evidence onto the skeptic. The tell is a claim delivered with a challenge to refute it, rather than support for it. The counter is to hold the line: the person asserting a claim owes the evidence, and a claim with no support can be dismissed with no support.
howToSpot: A claim is made, then you're told to disprove it
Failure to refute is treated as proof the claim is true
The claimant offers no positive evidence of their own

examples.text: "Ghosts are real — can you prove they're not?"
examples.explanation: The person claiming ghosts exist owes the evidence; inability to disprove isn't proof.

examples.text: "My product boosts memory. Show me a study proving it doesn't."
examples.explanation: The seller must demonstrate the benefit; skeptics don't have to disprove an unsupported claim.

examples.text: "I think the manager is sabotaging us. You can't prove he isn't, so I'm probably right."
examples.explanation: Lack of a disproof doesn't support the accusation — the burden is on the accuser.

refutation.title: Return the burden
refutation.text: Point out the claimant owes the evidence.
refutation.comeback: You made the claim, so the evidence is on you — not on me to disprove it.

refutation.title: Note unfalsifiability
refutation.text: Flag claims that can't be disproven by design.
refutation.comeback: If nothing could ever disprove it, 'you can't disprove it' means very little.

refutation.title: Dismiss the unsupported
refutation.text: State that no evidence means no reason to accept.
refutation.comeback: With no evidence offered, there's nothing here to accept in the first place.

avoidance: Support your own claims rather than daring others to refute them
Remember the burden of proof is on the one making the assertion
Don't treat 'unrefuted' as 'proven'

name: Appeal to Ignorance
hook: No one has ever proven the treatment doesn't work, so it clearly works.
oneLiner: Treating the absence of evidence against a claim as evidence for it.
deepDive: This fallacy concludes that a claim is true because it hasn't been proven false (or false because it hasn't been proven true). But 'we don't know' is not a conclusion in either direction — a lack of disproof is not proof. It exploits the gap in our knowledge and fills it with whatever the speaker prefers. It's closely tied to the burden of proof fallacy, but focuses specifically on turning ignorance into evidence. The nuance: in some contexts a *thorough* search that turns up nothing is genuinely informative ('we looked hard and found no side effects'). The fallacy is when mere absence of information — with no real search — is inflated into a positive conclusion. The counter is to insist that unknown means unknown, and to ask for actual positive evidence.
howToSpot: 'Not disproven' is treated as 'proven' (or vice versa)
A gap in knowledge is filled with the speaker's preferred conclusion
No positive evidence is offered — only the absence of the opposite

examples.text: "Nobody has proven aliens haven't visited Earth, so they must have."
examples.explanation: Absence of disproof isn't evidence of visits — the claim still needs positive support.

examples.text: "There's no proof the new hire is dishonest, so he must be completely trustworthy."
examples.explanation: Lack of evidence of dishonesty doesn't establish trustworthiness; it establishes nothing either way.

examples.text: "No study has shown this supplement is unsafe, therefore it's safe."
examples.explanation: Untested is not the same as proven safe — absence of findings isn't a clean bill of health.

refutation.title: Insist unknown means unknown
refutation.text: Refuse to convert ignorance into a conclusion.
refutation.comeback: Not being disproven isn't the same as being true — this is still an open question.

refutation.title: Ask for positive evidence
refutation.text: Request support for the claim itself.
refutation.comeback: What actual evidence is there for the claim, beyond the lack of evidence against it?

refutation.title: Check if a real search happened
refutation.text: Distinguish 'we looked and found nothing' from 'we never looked.'
refutation.comeback: Has anyone actually investigated this, or do we just not know yet?

avoidance: Treat 'unknown' as unknown, not as evidence for your preferred answer
Require positive evidence, not just the absence of contradiction
Distinguish a thorough search that found nothing from never having looked

name: Texas Sharpshooter
hook: I predicted three market crashes! (Out of the forty times I predicted a crash.)
oneLiner: Cherry-picking data clusters after the fact to fit a pattern you wanted to find.
deepDive: The name comes from a shooter who fires at a barn wall, then paints the target around the tightest cluster of holes — making random shots look like expert marksmanship. The fallacy works the same way: you gather data, ignore everything that doesn't fit, draw the 'target' around the hits, and declare a pattern. It ignores the misses, the base rate, and the fact that random data naturally contains clusters. It's rampant in claims about predictions, alternative medicine, and conspiracy 'evidence,' where successes are counted and failures quietly dropped. The tell is a striking pattern presented without the full dataset — no denominator, no mention of what didn't fit. The counter is to ask for everything: all the predictions, all the cases, the hits *and* the misses.
howToSpot: A pattern is highlighted while the data that doesn't fit is omitted
Only the 'hits' are counted; the misses and the base rate are ignored
The conclusion was drawn after the data was collected, to fit what was wanted

examples.text: "This psychic predicted the disaster!" (ignoring the hundreds of predictions that failed.)
examples.explanation: Counting only the one hit, out of many misses, manufactures a pattern from noise.

examples.text: "Everyone who took the remedy and recovered proves it works." (ignoring those who took it and didn't.)
examples.explanation: Selecting only the recoveries hides the failures needed to judge whether it actually helps.

examples.text: "Look how many championship teams wear red — red must cause winning."
examples.explanation: The red-wearing losers are left out; a cluster is highlighted and the rest ignored.

refutation.title: Ask for the full dataset
refutation.text: Request the misses as well as the hits.
refutation.comeback: How many times did it fail? I need the full picture, not just the successes.

refutation.title: Ask about the base rate
refutation.text: Probe how likely the pattern is by chance.
refutation.comeback: Out of how many total attempts? A few hits in a huge sample isn't remarkable.

refutation.title: Check the timing
refutation.text: Ask whether the pattern was predicted or found afterward.
refutation.comeback: Was this predicted in advance, or did you spot the pattern after the fact?

avoidance: Look at all the data, including the cases that don't fit your pattern
Ask for the base rate and the misses, not just the hits
Decide what you're testing before you collect the data
